title: Do Charters Damage The Teacher Pipeline
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene responds to a REACH report finding that cities with more charter schools produce fewer teachers from university prep programs. He opens with a firm caution that correlation is not causation, then asks what plausible link might exist. His answer is that charter operators favour untrained, short-stay alternative-route teachers, so prospective teachers who spend thirteen years watching the profession see a parade of beginners who never mature and a job reduced to implementing a canned curriculum. He adds that public systems in charter-heavy cities are often run down, which makes teaching look worse still. The piece is commentary on the teaching profession and its recruitment, offered as a hypothesis rather than a proven finding.
points: The REACH report links growth in urban charter sectors to fewer graduates from traditional teacher prep, especially in elementary, math and special education.
Greene flags the correlation-causation limit before offering any explanation, modelling cautious reading of education research.
His proposed mechanism is that teaching recruits its own members through years of observation, so a high-turnover, scripted charter workforce makes the job look unattractive.
Run-down public systems in charter-heavy cities compound the problem by making teachers labour harder with less respect and support.
quotes: Short version: in cities, when you get more charter schools, you get fewer teachers coming out of college and university teacher prep programs. Harris finds that elementary, math, and special ed suffer the most.
So charter schools and the teacher pipeline might very well have absolutely nothing to do with each other. We need to be clear on that right up front.

Charter businesses like teachers without traditional training, and they like temps with a high turnover (like Teach for America). Alternative path teachers tend to leave sooner, which suits charter businesses just fine.

No profession recruits its own members quite like teaching. Prospective teachers get to watch the profession for thirteen years. They have all that time to watch and think, "Wow, that looks awesome" or "May God forbid I ever wind up in that job.

So what might the effect be of watching a steady parade of mediocre beginners who never stick around to become mature professionals? Particularly in a charter where the teacher's job is to simply implement the program they're handed. Just how fun does reading a canned curriculum look?
Charters are the point of the spear in a general move to devalue the teaching profession, and a lack of interest in that profession would certainly be a predictable result.
